text: Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
reflection: The people of Jerusalem had gathered to hear God's law read aloud. As Ezra read and the Levites explained, the people understood how far they had fallen short, and they began to weep. But Nehemiah stopped them. He told them to go and celebrate, to eat and drink and share with those who had nothing. Then he gave the reason: "neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength." There is a time for sorrow over sin. But God did not want His people to stay in grief. Having heard His Word, they were to rejoice in His goodness. The joy of the Lord is not shallow happiness. It is a deep gladness rooted in who God is and what He has done. And it is strength. Joy gives us energy to keep going, courage to face hard days, and resilience when trouble comes. This month we will think about joy, praise, and worship. Begin by letting God's joy become your strength.
question: Where do you need the joy of the Lord to be your strength today?
prayer: Lord, the joy of the Lord is my strength. Where I am weak or downcast, fill me with joy rooted in You, and give me fresh courage for today. Amen.

text: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
reflection: Where is joy found? People search for it in many places: possessions, relationships, achievements, travel, and entertainment. Some of these bring moments of happiness. But David discovered where full joy lives: "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore." Fulness of joy. Not partial, not temporary, but complete. And it is found in God's presence. The pleasures at His right hand are for evermore. They do not fade or disappoint. Every other joy is a small stream. God Himself is the ocean. This does not mean earthly joys are wrong. They are gifts from Him. But they were never meant to carry the full weight of our happiness. Only God can do that. If you have been chasing joy and finding it slipping away, turn toward His presence. Spend time with Him. Let Him show you the path of life. Full joy is waiting there.
question: What earthly joy have you been expecting to satisfy you that only God can?
prayer: Lord, in Your presence is fulness of joy, and at Your right hand are pleasures for evermore. Thank You for every good gift, but satisfy me with Yourself today. Amen.

text: Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
reflection: Psalm 100 is a short song of praise, and it gives a surprising instruction about serving God: "Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Many people think of serving God as a heavy duty, something we do out of obligation. But the psalmist says to serve with gladness. Joy and service belong together. Why? Because we serve a good God who has been kind to us. We serve out of gratitude, not fear. We serve because we love Him. And our service is not to a harsh master but to a loving Father. The psalm continues by reminding us that He made us, we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture. That is reason for gladness. Serving with gladness changes everything. It turns chores into worship and duties into delights. Whatever work is in front of you today, whether at home, at work, or in your community, do it gladly as service to the Lord. Let joy fill your work.
question: How could you do today's work gladly, as service to the Lord?
prayer: Lord, I want to serve You with gladness and come before You with singing. Let my work today flow from gratitude, not fear, and let it be done for You. Amen.

text: Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name.
reflection: Psalm 100 continues with directions for approaching God: "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name." The picture is of worshippers coming to the temple, passing through the gates and into the courts. They did not walk in casually. They came with thanks and praise on their lips. Thanksgiving and praise are the doorway into God's presence. When we begin with gratitude, our hearts open. We remember His goodness. Our worries shrink in the light of His faithfulness. Many of us approach God with a list of requests. That is not wrong. He invites us to bring our needs. But this psalm teaches us to begin with thanks. Before you ask for anything today, thank Him for something. Then praise Him for who He is. You may find that your requests look different after you have entered through the gates of thanksgiving. Bless His name today.
question: Before you ask God for anything today, what could you thank and praise Him for?
prayer: Lord, I enter Your gates with thanksgiving and Your courts with praise. Before I bring You my requests, I thank You for who You are and all You have done. Amen.

text: This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
reflection: This verse is often sung, often quoted, and easy to say. But its original setting gives it depth. Psalm 118 celebrates God's rescue. The psalmist had been surrounded by enemies and pushed hard, nearly falling. The stone the builders rejected had become the cornerstone. In other words, what people threw away, God made central. Then comes the joyful declaration: "This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it." Every day is a day the Lord has made. Not just the good ones. Not just the days when everything goes right. This day, the one you are living right now, is His. He made it, and He is present in it. Rejoicing in it is a choice. It does not depend on everything being perfect. It depends on recognizing whose day it is. Whatever today holds, it belongs to God. Choose to rejoice and be glad in it.
question: How could you rejoice in today, even if it is not an easy one, because it is the day the Lord has made?
prayer: Lord, this is the day which You have made. Easy or hard, it belongs to You. Help me rejoice and be glad in it, knowing whose day it is. Amen.

text: Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
reflection: Paul wrote the letter to the Philippians from prison. He did not know whether he would live or die. Yet joy runs through the whole letter, and here he says it twice: "Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice." Paul repeats it because he knows it is hard to believe. Rejoice always? Even in prison? Even in uncertainty? Yes, because the joy he speaks of is in the Lord. It is not joy in circumstances. Circumstances change. Joy in the Lord does not. Paul could not rejoice in his chains, but he could rejoice in Christ. He could rejoice that the gospel was spreading, that God was faithful, and that nothing could separate him from God's love. This kind of joy is a decision and a discipline. It turns our attention from what is wrong to who God is. What would it look like for you to rejoice in the Lord today, even if your circumstances are hard? Paul says it again: rejoice.
question: What situation are you in today where you could still choose to rejoice in the Lord?
prayer: Lord, I choose to rejoice in You always, and again I say, rejoice. My joy does not rest on my circumstances but on who You are. Fill me with that joy today. Amen.

text: Rejoice evermore.
reflection: This is one of the shortest verses in the Bible. Just two words: "Rejoice evermore." It comes in a list of brief instructions near the end of Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks. Quench not the Spirit. Each command is short, but each one reaches into every part of life. Evermore means always, continually, without stopping. It is not occasional joy, saved for special events. It is a steady undercurrent of gladness that runs beneath everything. How is that possible? Not by pretending. Not by forcing a smile. It comes from remembering what God has done and who He is, again and again. The Thessalonian believers were facing persecution. Paul was not writing to people with easy lives. Yet he called them to rejoice evermore, because their joy was anchored in Christ. Today, let joy be your background music. Return to it throughout the day. Rejoice evermore.
question: How could you return to joy again and again throughout today?
prayer: Lord, help me rejoice evermore. Let a steady gladness run beneath every part of my day, as I remember again and again who You are. Amen.

text: I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth.
reflection: David wrote Psalm 34 after a frightening escape. He had pretended to be insane before a Philistine king to save his life. It was not a proud moment. Yet when he was safe, he did not dwell on his fear or embarrassment. He began with praise: "I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth." At all times. In good times and hard times. When things go well and when they fall apart. David decided that praise would be his constant response. Continually in my mouth. It would not be occasional but habitual. This is a choice that shapes a life. Complaining can become a habit, and so can praise. What fills our mouths often fills our hearts. When we make a habit of blessing God, we begin to see His goodness everywhere. Today, try to make praise continual. Thank Him for small things. Bless Him in ordinary moments. Let His praise be in your mouth all day.
question: How could praise become your first response to whatever happens today?
prayer: Lord, I will bless You at all times; Your praise shall continually be in my mouth. Make praise my habit, and let it shape the way I see everything today. Amen.

text: O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together.
reflection: Praise is personal, but it is also meant to be shared. David followed his own declaration of praise with an invitation: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt his name together." To magnify means to make large. A magnifying glass does not make something bigger than it is. It helps us see how big it really is. When we magnify the Lord, we are not adding to His greatness. We are helping ourselves and others see it more clearly. And David wants company. Let us exalt his name together. There is something powerful about shared praise. When we worship alongside others, our faith is strengthened. We hear what God has done in their lives. We are reminded that we are not alone. Joy multiplies when it is shared. Today, invite someone to magnify the Lord with you. Share something God has done. Ask what He has done for them. Exalt His name together.
question: What has God done for you that you could share with someone and praise Him for together?
prayer: Lord, I want to magnify You with others and exalt Your name together. Give me an opportunity today to share what You have done, and let our joy multiply. Amen.

text: O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation.
reflection: Psalm 95 opens with an exuberant invitation: "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation." A joyful noise. Not necessarily a polished performance, but a glad sound. God is not looking for perfect voices. He delights in joyful hearts. Many people feel shy about singing. But this psalm is not about talent. It is about gladness overflowing into sound. And notice the reason for the joy: the rock of our salvation. A rock is solid, unshakable, and dependable. Our salvation rests on God, who does not move or change. That is worth making noise about. Throughout Scripture, God's people sang. They sang at the Red Sea, in the temple, in prison cells, and on the road. Singing lifts the heart and focuses the mind on God. Today, whether in the car, at home, or under your breath, sing to the Lord. Make a joyful noise to the Rock of your salvation.
question: Where could you sing to the Lord today, even quietly, with a glad heart?
prayer: Lord, Rock of my salvation, I make a joyful noise to You. Thank You that You delight in a glad heart, not a perfect voice. Let me sing to You today. Amen.

text: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker.
reflection: The first verses of Psalm 95 are loud and joyful, with singing and shouting. But then the tone shifts: "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker." Worship has more than one posture. Sometimes it is exuberant celebration. Sometimes it is quiet reverence. Bowing and kneeling are postures of humility. They acknowledge that God is great and we are small. He is the Maker, and we are what He made. Kneeling before Him is not humiliation. It is recognition of who He truly is. There is freedom in this. When we bow before God, we stop trying to be in control. We release the burden of running the universe. We rest in His authority. Whether or not you physically kneel, you can bow your heart today. Take a quiet moment to acknowledge His greatness. Let reverence fill your heart. He is your Maker, and He is worthy of your worship.
question: What need for control could you release as you bow your heart before your Maker today?
prayer: Lord my Maker, I bow and kneel before You. You are great, and I am Yours. Take my need for control as I bow my heart before You today. Amen.

text: O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth.
reflection: Psalm 96 calls the whole earth to praise God. In the middle of it is this invitation: "O worship the LORD in the beauty of holiness: fear before him, all the earth." The beauty of holiness. Holiness is not dull or grim. It is beautiful. God's holiness, His perfect purity and goodness, is the most beautiful thing in existence. And when we worship Him, we are drawn into that beauty. Some think of holiness as a list of rules. But true holiness is the radiant goodness of God's character. It is love without selfishness, truth without falsehood, and justice without corruption. When we glimpse it, we are moved to worship. The verse also says, fear before him. This is not terror but awe, the trembling wonder of standing before Someone infinitely greater. Beauty and awe belong together in worship. Today, spend a few moments reflecting on God's holiness. Let its beauty draw you to worship.
question: What about God's holiness could you reflect on today until it moves your heart to worship?
prayer: Lord, I worship You in the beauty of holiness. Your goodness is radiant and pure. Open my eyes to the beauty of who You are, and fill me with awe today. Amen.

text: Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name.
reflection: Psalm 103 begins with David speaking to himself: "Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name." David is giving instructions to his own soul. Sometimes our souls need to be told what to do. Our emotions may be flat. Our minds may be distracted. Our hearts may feel heavy. So David commands his soul to praise. This is not hypocrisy. It is leadership of oneself. And he wants all of himself involved: all that is within me. Not just his lips, but his mind, his heart, his emotions, and his will. Whole-person worship. Many people wait until they feel like praising God. But feelings often follow actions. When we choose to bless the Lord, our hearts often warm along the way. Today, if your soul feels sluggish, speak to it as David did. Tell your soul to bless the Lord. Then bring everything within you into His praise.
question: What would it mean today to tell your soul to bless the Lord, even before your feelings follow?
prayer: Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless His holy name. Lord, I bring all of myself to worship You today, whatever I am feeling. Amen.

text: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits…
reflection: David continued his instruction to his soul: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits." Forgetfulness is one of the great enemies of praise. We are quick to remember our problems and slow to remember God's blessings. A single bad day can erase the memory of a hundred good ones. So David reminds himself to remember. And then he lists the benefits: God forgives all our iniquities, heals our diseases, redeems our life from destruction, crowns us with lovingkindness and tender mercies, and satisfies our mouths with good things. Each one is a reason for praise. One helpful practice is to make your own list. Write down the ways God has blessed you. Forgiveness, provision, protection, answered prayers, people He has placed in your life, and moments when He showed up. When you see them written out, praise comes more easily. Today, forget not. Count His benefits, and bless Him for each one.
question: What benefits of God could you list today and thank Him for one by one?
prayer: Lord, I will not forget all Your benefits. Thank You for forgiving, healing, redeeming, and crowning me with lovingkindness and tender mercies. Amen.

text: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
reflection: The book of Psalms ends with a burst of praise. Psalm 150 calls for praise with trumpets, harps, timbrels, strings, organs, and cymbals. And then the final verse widens the invitation to include everyone and everything: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD." Every thing that hath breath. If you are breathing, you have a reason and a calling to praise God. Your breath itself is His gift. Every inhale and exhale is a reminder that He sustains your life. This is a fitting end to the Psalms. The book includes laments, confessions, cries for help, and questions. But it ends in praise. It is as if the whole journey of faith, with all its ups and downs, finally arrives at worship. Wherever you are in your own journey, praise is where it leads. Take a deep breath today. Notice it. Then use that breath to praise the Lord.
question: How could you use some of today's breaths to praise the Lord?
prayer: Lord, every breath I take is Your gift. Let everything that has breath praise You, and let my breath praise You today. Amen.

text: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
reflection: Jesus was talking with a Samaritan woman at a well. She raised a long-standing debate: where should people worship? Samaritans said on their mountain. Jews said in Jerusalem. Jesus answered with something deeper: "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." True worship is not limited to a particular place. Because God is Spirit, He can be worshipped anywhere. What matters is not the location but the heart. In spirit means from the inside, with genuine heart engagement, not just outward forms. In truth means according to who God really is, as He has revealed Himself. Both are needed. Spirit without truth can become emotion without substance. Truth without spirit can become cold and empty. Jesus invites us to worship with both our hearts and our minds fully engaged. You can worship God today wherever you are, in a kitchen, an office, or a hospital room. Bring Him your heart, and bring Him the truth.
question: How could you worship God today with both your heart and your mind, wherever you are?
prayer: Father, You are seeking those who worship You in spirit and in truth. Engage my heart and fill my mind with what is true about You, wherever I am today. Amen.

text: These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.
reflection: On the night before His death, Jesus spoke at length with His disciples. He talked about the vine and the branches, about abiding in Him and keeping His commandments. Then He explained why He was telling them all this: "These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full." Jesus wanted His followers to have His joy. Not a lesser joy or a borrowed one, but His own. The same joy He had in His relationship with the Father. And He wanted it to be full, complete, overflowing. This is remarkable timing. Jesus was hours away from the cross. Yet He was speaking about joy. His joy did not depend on easy circumstances. It came from His union with the Father and His obedience to the Father's will. That is the joy He offers us. It is found in abiding in Him and walking in His ways. Stay close to Jesus today, and let His joy fill you.
question: What would it look like to abide in Jesus today so that His joy fills you?
prayer: Lord Jesus, You spoke so that Your joy might remain in me and my joy might be full. Help me abide in You today, and fill me with Your joy. Amen.

text: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.
reflection: Paul ends a long section of his letter to the Romans with a prayer-blessing: "Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost." Notice the flow. God is the God of hope. He fills us with joy and peace. This happens in believing, as we trust Him. And the result is that we abound in hope, overflowing with it. All of this comes through the power of the Holy Ghost, not our own effort. Joy and peace are not things we have to produce. They are gifts God pours in as we trust Him. Believing is the channel. When we stop trusting, the flow slows. When we trust Him more, joy and peace increase. And they overflow into hope that others can see. If you feel empty of joy today, ask the God of hope to fill you. Then put your trust in Him again. Let Him do the filling.
question: Where do you need God to fill you with joy and peace as you trust Him today?
prayer: God of hope, fill me with all joy and peace in believing, that I may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Ghost. Renew my trust in You today. Amen.

text: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
reflection: Nights can be long. Grief feels heavier in the dark. Worries grow louder when everything else is quiet. David knew such nights, and he wrote this promise: "weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning." Weeping is real. David does not dismiss it. Night is real. But night is not permanent. Morning comes. The sun rises. And with it, joy returns. David had experienced God's discipline and then His restoration. He had known sorrow and then celebration. And he learned that sorrow is temporary for God's people. The verse begins with a contrast too: "his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life." God's favour, not His anger, is the lasting thing. Some nights last longer than one evening. Some seasons of weeping stretch for months or years. But they are still nights, and morning is still coming. If you are in a night season, hold on. Joy is on its way.
question: If you are in a night season, what helps you hold on until the morning?
prayer: Lord, weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning. If I am in the night, help me hold on, trusting that morning is coming. Amen.

text: The LORD hath done great things for us; whereof we are glad.
reflection: Psalm 126 was sung by people who had returned from exile. For years they had lived in Babylon, far from home. Then God brought them back, and it felt like a dream. Their mouths were filled with laughter and their tongues with singing. Even the nations around them noticed and said, the Lord has done great things for them. And the people answered, "The LORD hath done great things for us; whereof we are glad." Gladness flows from remembering what God has done. When we forget His works, joy fades. When we recall them, joy returns. These returning exiles could have focused on the ruins they found or the hard work ahead. Instead, they celebrated God's faithfulness. What great things has God done for you? Perhaps He rescued you from something, provided when you had nothing, healed a wound, or brought you home. Take time today to name them. Then rejoice. The Lord has done great things for you.
question: What great things has God done for you that you could name and rejoice in today?
prayer: Lord, You have done great things for me, and I am glad. Help me remember Your works today, and let my remembering turn into joy and praise. Amen.

text: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
reflection: Psalm 126 ends with a farming image: "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy." In ancient Israel, sowing could be a sorrowful task. In times of famine, farmers had to take precious grain that could feed their families and bury it in the ground, trusting it would grow. They sowed with tears, unsure of the outcome. But the harvest came, and with it, joy. This verse speaks to anyone doing something hard in faith. Perhaps you are praying for someone who seems far from God. Perhaps you are caring for someone through a long illness. Perhaps you are working faithfully without seeing results. You may be sowing in tears. The promise is that tears are not the end. Seeds sown in faith, even with weeping, will bring a harvest of joy. The next verse adds that the one who goes forth weeping shall doubtless come again rejoicing. Doubtless. Keep sowing. The harvest is coming.
question: What are you sowing in tears that you could keep sowing in faith today?
prayer: Lord, those who sow in tears shall reap in joy. Even when I am weeping, help me keep sowing faithfully, trusting You for the harvest. Amen.

text: To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that he might be glorified.
reflection: Isaiah 61 describes the mission of God's anointed servant. He comes to bring good news to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, and to set captives free. Then come three beautiful exchanges: "to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness." In ancient times, mourners put ashes on their heads. God replaces those ashes with a crown of beauty. Mourners went without oil on their skin. God anoints them with the oil of joy. And for a heavy, burdened spirit, He gives a garment of praise, like a festive robe to wear. Jesus read from this chapter in His hometown synagogue and said it was fulfilled in Him. He is the One who makes these exchanges. A garment is something you put on. When heaviness weighs on your spirit, you can put on praise. Not to deny your sorrow, but to let God's goodness cover it. Bring Him your ashes today. Receive His beauty.
question: What heaviness could you bring to Jesus today in exchange for the garment of praise?
prayer: Lord, You give beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. I bring You my heaviness, and I put on praise. Amen.

text: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
reflection: Isaiah 12 is a short song of praise that God's people would sing in the day of salvation. Its heart is this verse: "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song." God is not just the source of salvation. He is salvation. Salvation is not merely something He gives; it is found in Him. And because of that, the singer can say, I will trust, and not be afraid. Trust and fearlessness flow from knowing who God is. Then comes a lovely phrase: my strength and my song. Strength is what we need to keep going. Song is what we sing when we are glad. God is both. He gives us the power to endure and the joy to celebrate. He carries us through hard times and fills our mouths with praise afterward. Make this verse your song today. God is your salvation, your strength, and your song.
question: What fear could you answer today by declaring that God is your strength and your song?
prayer: Lord, You are my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. You are my strength and my song. Let this be the song of my heart today. Amen.

text: The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him.
reflection: The Israelites had just walked through the Red Sea on dry ground. They watched the waters crash down on Pharaoh's army. They were free. And the first thing they did was sing. Moses led them in a song, and in it they declared, "The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him." This is the first recorded song in the Bible. It came straight out of a moment of deliverance. Praise was the natural response to rescue. Notice how personal it is. My strength. My song. My salvation. My God. My father's God. They had heard about the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Now they knew Him for themselves. When God rescues us, praise should follow. Think of a time God delivered you. Let that memory turn into a song today. Exalt your father's God, who has become your God too.
question: What deliverance in your life could you remember and turn into a song today?
prayer: Lord, You are my strength and song, and You have become my salvation. As I remember how You have rescued me, let my thanks rise up in praise today. Amen.

text: And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod.
reflection: When the ark of God was finally brought into Jerusalem, King David could not contain his joy. "And David danced before the LORD with all his might." He was not concerned with looking dignified. He set aside his royal robes and wore a simple linen ephod. He leaped and danced in front of the whole city. His wife Michal watched from a window and despised him for it. She thought he had embarrassed himself. But David answered that he was dancing before the Lord, and he would become even more undignified if that is what worship required. David worshipped with all his might. Not half-hearted. Not reserved. Not worried about what others thought. His whole being was caught up in celebrating God. Worship can take many forms, and not everyone expresses joy the same way. But the question is worth asking: do we hold back from God because we care too much about how we look? Today, give Him your whole heart.
question: Is fear of what others think holding back your worship, and how could you give God your whole heart today?
prayer: Lord, David worshipped You with all his might and did not care how he looked. Free me from fear of others' opinions, and let me worship You with my whole heart. Amen.

text: And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
reflection: Psalm 40 begins with David waiting patiently for the Lord. God heard his cry, lifted him out of a horrible pit and miry clay, and set his feet on a rock. Then David says, "And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God." A new song. Not an old, worn-out tune sung from habit, but fresh praise born from a fresh experience of God's rescue. And notice who gave it: he hath put. Even the song is a gift from God. He gives us the rescue and then the words to praise Him for it. Then comes a beautiful result: "many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD." Our praise is a witness. When others see what God has done in our lives and hear us thank Him, their faith is stirred. Your story of God's faithfulness could help someone else trust Him. What new song has God given you? Sing it today, and let others hear.
question: What story of God's faithfulness in your life could you share with someone today?
prayer: Lord, You lifted me out of the pit and put a new song in my mouth. Let my praise be a witness, and help me share my story so that others may trust You. Amen.

text: Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee.
reflection: What could be better than life itself? For most people, life is the most precious thing they have. Yet David, writing in a dry wilderness while fleeing his enemies, declared, "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee." Lovingkindness is God's faithful, covenant love. It is loyal love that never lets go. David said it was better than life. If he had to choose between living without God's love and dying with it, he would choose God's love. This is a remarkable statement. It shows how deeply David valued his relationship with God. Everything else, even life, came second. And because of this, he could not help but praise. My lips shall praise thee. When we realize how great God's love is, praise flows naturally. Today, reflect on God's lovingkindness. It is steady, faithful, and unending. It is better than anything else you have. Let it move your lips to praise.
question: What would change in your day if you truly believed God's lovingkindness is better than life?
prayer: Lord, Your lovingkindness is better than life; therefore my lips shall praise You. Let the greatness of Your love move me to worship today. Amen.

text: Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.
reflection: Jesus told three stories in a row: a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son. Each one ended in celebration when the lost was found. After the story of the coin, He said, "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Heaven rejoices. When one person turns back to God, there is celebration in His presence. This tells us something wonderful about God's heart. He is not reluctant to receive sinners. He is not grudging in His forgiveness. He is glad. Joy fills heaven when the lost come home. Jesus told these stories to religious leaders who complained that He welcomed sinners. He wanted them to see God's heart. And He wanted them to join the celebration instead of grumbling. Do we rejoice when someone comes to God? Or do we hold them at a distance? Today, share in heaven's joy. Pray for someone who is lost, and celebrate every return.
question: Who could you pray for today, longing for them to return to God?
prayer: Lord, there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents. Give me Your glad heart for the lost. I pray for those I know who are far from You. Amen.

text: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.
reflection: We often think of praising God. Less often do we think of God rejoicing over us. Yet Zephaniah paints exactly that picture: "The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing." Read it slowly. God is in your midst. He is mighty. He saves. And then He rejoices over you with joy. He rests in His love, quiet and content. And He sings over you. The Creator of the universe singing over His people. It is a picture of a parent delighting in a child, or a bridegroom rejoicing over a bride. Many people carry a sense that God is disappointed in them, or merely tolerates them. This verse says something different. For those who are His, God delights. He rejoices. He sings. Let that truth sink in today. You are not only called to rejoice in God. He rejoices over you.
question: How might your day change if you let it sink in that God rejoices over you?
prayer: Lord, You are in the midst of Your people, mighty to save, and You rejoice over me with singing. Help me believe that You delight in me, and rest in Your love today. Amen.

text: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High…
reflection: Psalm 92 carries a title in the original: a psalm or song for the sabbath day. It begins with this simple statement: "It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High." A good thing. Giving thanks is not just appropriate. It is good. Good for God, who deserves it. Good for us, because it lifts our hearts. Good for others, who are encouraged by our gratitude. The next verse adds when to do it: to shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night. Morning and evening. Starting and ending the day with thanks frames everything in between. In the morning, we look ahead with gratitude for His love. At night, we look back with gratitude for His faithfulness. Try it today. Before your day begins, thank God for His love. Before you sleep, thank Him for His faithfulness. It is a good thing.
question: How could you begin and end today with thanks to the Lord?
prayer: Lord, it is a good thing to give thanks to You. Let me declare Your lovingkindness in the morning and Your faithfulness every night. Amen.

text: Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created.
reflection: In Revelation 4, John is given a glimpse of heaven's throne room. He sees God seated in glory, surrounded by worshippers. Twenty-four elders cast their crowns before the throne and say, "Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory and honour and power: for thou hast created all things, and for thy pleasure they are and were created." This is worship at its purest. The elders do not ask for anything. They simply declare God's worth. And the reason they give is creation. He made all things. Everything exists because He willed it. Casting their crowns shows that any honour they have belongs to Him. This month we have thought about joy, praise, and worship. Revelation shows where it all leads. Worship is not just something we do on earth. It is the eternal activity of heaven. Every song we sing now is practice for that day. End this month by joining the elders. Tell God He is worthy. Lay your crowns at His feet.
question: What could you tell God today about why He is worthy of your praise?
prayer: Lord, You are worthy to receive glory and honour and power, for You created all things. I join heaven's worship today and lay my crowns before You. Amen.
